targets.title: Do defaults save lives?
targets.evidence_quote: In two well-powered samples (N = 1920), we conducted a close replication of the default effect in Johnson and Goldstein (2003) and in Johnson, Bellman, and Lohse (2002).
targets.outcome_quote: We successfully replicated Johnson and Goldstein (2003).
targets.outcome_reasoning: Overall verdict confirms this target despite smaller effects; both samples contributed to Part 1.

targets.authors: Johnson, E. J., Bellman, S., & Lohse, G. L.
targets.title: Defaults, framing and privacy: Why opting in-opting out.
targets.evidence_quote: Second, we added a conceptual replication of Johnson et al. (2002).
targets.outcome_quote: The findings across direct and conceptual replication of Johnson et al. (2002) provide mixed support to the original study’s assertion.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The explicit aggregate verdict across direct and conceptual replications is mixed. The abstract failure verdict covers the direct attempt and does not supersede this fuller aggregation; both samples contributed to Part 2 and Sample 2 also to Extension 2.

targets.evidence_quote: We based our extension on Van Dalen and Henkens (2014) who found that organ donation rates were higher when the option was temporary and would have to be renewed than when the default option was to donate.
targets.outcome_quote: In the first extension, we predicted that people would be more inclined to become donors when consent to organ donation is temporary. We found no evidence that consent varied between the temporary and permanent conditions.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Extension 1 explicitly retests this cited temporal-choice finding in Sample 1. The supplied cache lacks its reference entry; title and DOI cannot be copied.
